title: From the dear, grief (209–216)
hook: from what is dear comes grief, from what is dear comes fear; one free of it has neither

segments.voice: Yesterday, good company: follow the wise, as the moon follows the stars. Your line was keep good company. Who did you spend a few minutes with? Day one hundred ninety-nine, and chapter sixteen begins.

A stranger's phone falls in a lake, and nobody loses sleep. A coworker's cousin has surgery, and the day goes on. But a parent's kid is ten minutes late, and the stomach starts to knot. A dog limps, and the whole evening goes gray. The things we love are exactly the things that can hurt us, and still, people go on loving. Chapter sixteen of the Dhammapada looks at that trade with unusual honesty. Today: from the dear, grief.
screen: `A STRANGER'S PHONE IN THE LAKE.` → `A KID, TEN MINUTES LATE.` → `WHAT WE LOVE CAN HURT US.`

segments.voice: Chapter sixteen is called Piyavagga. Piya means dear, beloved, precious. Müller titled it pleasure, but dear is closer. Verse two twelve, in his words: "From pleasure comes grief, from pleasure comes fear; he who is free from pleasure knows neither grief nor fear." In Pali it's: from what is dear comes sorrow, from what is dear comes fear. Then the next four verses repeat it with other words: from affection, from lust, from love, from craving. Five times, the same shape. There's a story in the Udāna, one of the early collections. Visākhā, a devoted lay follower of the Buddha, came to him in wet clothes and wet hair, grieving a grandchild who had died. He asked her: would you like as many children and grandchildren as there are people in this city? Yes, she said. And how many people die in this city each day? Many, she said. Then, he answered gently, you'd never be without wet clothes and wet hair. Those who have a hundred dear ones have a hundred sorrows. Those who have none have none. This is hard teaching, and verse two eleven goes further still, in Müller's words: "Let, therefore, no man love anything; loss of the beloved is evil." Buddhists read that in more than one way. Some take it strictly, as monastics do when they leave close family ties behind. Some teachers read it as being about grasping: love fully, hold loosely, knowing that everything dear will change. The tradition's own loving-kindness, metta, wishes all beings well without clutching any of them. Either way, the verses tell the truth about love's cost.
screen: `PIYA — DEAR, BELOVED.` · `FIVE TIMES, THE SAME SHAPE.` · `VISĀKHĀ IN WET CLOTHES.` · `LOVE FULLY, HOLD LOOSELY.` · then, large: `FROM THE DEAR, GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind one person, animal or thing you love. Let yourself feel the love, warmly, fully. Then notice whether there's a small grip in it too: a tightness, a fear of losing it. Don't push the love away. Just soften the grip, the way you'd open a fist that was holding a bird too tightly. Wish them well: may you be safe, may you be at ease, whatever happens. Love without clutching. Then rest in the breath, open-handed. The bell holds the time.
From the dear. Verse two twelve: from what is dear comes grief, from what is dear comes fear; one who is free of it knows neither.
Your line: from the dear, grief. Today, love one thing without grasping: enjoy it fully, and let it be free to change. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics leave close family ties behind, and some teachers present these verses to lay people as a call to love without clinging, and to meet loss with the understanding that everything dear will change.

fork.reveal: she said yes. then he asked how many die there each day: many. "you'd never be without wet clothes and wet hair."

original.note: Pali: dear, beloved — piyato jāyatī soko, from the dear arises sorrow.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't love anything, and you won't get hurt.
what it means: everything dear can bring grief and fear; the teaching tells the cost honestly, and some read it as love without grasping.
what a scholar hears: Müller's pleasure renders piya, dear; the Visākhā story is in the Udāna (8.8).

Editor review 2026-10-01: SERIOUS fix: the teach said 'the verses don't forbid love', but verse 211 (Müller) says 'Let, therefore, no man love anything'; it is now quoted and the readings are attributed to some readers rather than stated as fact. Also: verse 212 alone does not repeat five times (212–216 do); cut 'greatest lay supporter'; hook no longer assumes the listener has a kid and a dog or says 'everyone knows'.
